acceptable.choice: Keep the relationship data in Postgres and precompute each user's top-N recommendations in a background job (using the existing Redis/BullMQ queues), storing them in a Postgres table or a per-user array/jsonb row that is read by primary key
acceptable.why: Serving becomes a single indexed lookup that easily stays under 300 ms, and it adds no new datastore, language or vendor.

acceptable.choice: Recompute incrementally: when a membership, team or project changes, enqueue recomputation for the affected users, and run a periodic full or partial rebuild as a safety net
acceptable.why: People-you-may-know tolerates minutes-to-hours of staleness, so event-driven recomputation keeps compute cost proportional to activity rather than to total users.

acceptable.choice: Compute on demand with a 2-hop SQL query (self-joins or a recursive CTE with a depth limit, deduplication and GROUP BY candidate ORDER BY shared-count), cache the result in Redis with a TTL, and precompute only for active users
acceptable.why: This is the cheapest version to ship first and works well when per-user fan-out is bounded by indexes and degree caps.

acceptable.choice: Run the heavy traversal queries against a Postgres read replica, or during off-peak batches
acceptable.why: The fan-out queries then don't compete with the transactional workload on the primary.

acceptable.choice: Write the traversal as raw SQL through Prisma ($queryRaw or TypedSQL) or a thin query builder such as Kysely, inside the existing TypeScript code base
acceptable.why: Prisma's model API can't express recursive or aggregate graph queries well, but raw SQL keeps the work in the team's language and tooling.

acceptable.choice: If batch SQL turns out to be too slow, run an in-memory adjacency graph (CSR in typed arrays, a few hundred MB for 40M edges) in a dedicated Node/TypeScript worker that writes results back to Postgres
acceptable.why: This is a measured escalation that stays in TypeScript and avoids a second system of record.

acceptable.choice: Stop at 2 hops for ranking, and use hop 3 only as a fallback for users with few 2-hop candidates
acceptable.why: 3-hop neighbourhoods in team/project graphs cover a large part of the graph and rank poorly, so limiting hops cuts cost and often improves relevance.

ruled_out.choice: Migrating relationship data to Neo4j (self-hosted on Fly.io)
ruled_out.why: Nobody on the team has run a JVM in production, and it adds a stateful cluster to operate plus a dual-write/CDC sync problem, for a 40M-edge graph that Postgres handles.

ruled_out.choice: Managed graph DB now (Neo4j Aura, Memgraph Cloud, TigerGraph Cloud)
ruled_out.why: It adds a second source of truth to keep consistent, a new query language (Cypher/GSQL), a significant fixed monthly cost and cross-provider latency from Fly.io, without any measurement showing Postgres plus precomputation is insufficient.
The team isn't on AWS, so it means cross-cloud latency and egress, VPC setup and a cost floor that conflicts with keeping the bill growing slower than revenue.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the API or the recommendation service in Go (or Java/Rust) for performance
ruled_out.why: The bottleneck is the data access pattern and the fan-out, not language speed, and a rewrite hurts shipping speed and the TypeScript-only hiring plan; one dev's Go experience doesn't justify a second production language.

ruled_out.choice: Live, unbounded 3-hop recursive CTE executed on every page load
ruled_out.why: Fan-out from high-degree users and large teams (supernodes) makes latency unpredictable and can blow far past 300 ms while also loading the primary database.

ruled_out.choice: Storing the full adjacency graph in Redis (sets/sorted sets with SUNION/ZUNIONSTORE) as the primary graph store
ruled_out.why: It needs several GB of RAM-priced storage and a second copy of the data to keep in sync; Redis belongs as a cache for results, not as the graph.

ruled_out.choice: Apache AGE or similar graph extensions on Postgres
ruled_out.why: They usually aren't available on managed Postgres providers and offer no real advantage over plain SQL for a bounded 2–3-hop count query.

ruled_out.choice: Spark GraphX / distributed graph processing frameworks
ruled_out.why: This is massive operational overkill for 2M nodes and 40M edges, and the stack is outside the team's skills.

must_mention: Recommendation: stay on Postgres. 2M users and 40M edges is small, and a graph database is not needed at this scale.
The 300 ms target is best met by precomputing or caching recommendations rather than traversing the graph on every request; this matters more than the choice of database.
PYMK can be slightly stale, so asynchronous recomputation through the existing Redis queues is a good fit.
Supernodes (large teams or projects, highly connected users) dominate the cost; cap fan-out, sample, or down-weight big groups (for example, Adamic-Adar-style weighting).
3 hops explodes combinatorially (an average degree of ~20–40 gives tens of thousands of paths per user, and far more for hubs); suggest 2 hops as the primary signal.
Need the right indexes on the edge/membership table (e.g. composite (user_id, team_id) and (team_id, user_id)), and exclude existing connections and the user themself.
Language: no. TypeScript/Node is fine because the work is I/O- and query-bound; a rewrite in Go would hurt hiring and velocity for no measured gain.
Prisma's model API won't express this well, so use raw SQL or TypedSQL for the traversal query.
Measure first: prototype the query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-shaped data, and look at p95/p99 latency for the highest-degree users, not the average.
Name the conditions that would justify revisiting a graph DB later, such as many varied deep-traversal features, real-time freshness requirements, or graph size orders of magnitude larger.
red_flags: Recommending Neo4j or another graph DB as the default answer because 'it's a graph problem', ignoring the scale, the team's lack of JVM experience, sync complexity and cost
Suggesting a Go/Rust/Java rewrite or a polyglot microservice for speed, without evidence that the CPU is the bottleneck
Proposing live recursive 3-hop queries per request with no depth limit, deduplication, degree caps or caching, and claiming they will meet 300 ms
Ignoring supernode/high-degree users and quoting only average-case latency
Proposing dual-writes between Postgres and a new store without addressing consistency, backfill and failure handling
Recommending infrastructure that grows the fixed cloud bill substantially (dedicated graph clusters, large Redis instances holding the whole graph) for a seed-stage company
Claiming that Postgres 'can't do graphs' or that a graph DB is needed above some small edge count
Precomputing the full top-K for all 2M users nightly without considering the storage size (e.g. 2M × 100 rows) or incremental and active-user-only strategies
Using Prisma's nested relation queries or N+1 traversal in application code to walk hops
unknowns: Shape of the data: is it user↔team/project membership (bipartite) or direct user↔user edges, and is the 40M figure memberships or derived pairs?
Degree distribution: the size of the largest teams and projects and the most-connected users, which sets worst-case fan-out
Freshness requirement: whether a new teammate must show up in recommendations within seconds, or whether hours is fine
Read traffic (QPS for the PYMK widget) and the share of users who are active, which decides between precompute-all, precompute-active and compute-on-demand
Measured latency of a 2-hop and 3-hop query on production-shaped data at p95/p99, using EXPLAIN ANALYZE
The managed Postgres provider and plan: whether read replicas are available, extensions, memory and IOPS headroom
Whether product truly needs 3 hops, or whether 2 hops plus fallbacks gives equal or better relevance
Expected graph growth and whether other graph-heavy features are planned, which could later change the case for a dedicated graph store
Privacy and visibility rules (blocked users, private projects, cross-tenant boundaries) that must be applied during candidate generation
